title: Receiving well
hook: receive gladly, and let the giver see it (On Benefits 2.22)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was giving well: freely, promptly, and without reminding. Your line was give, then forget.

Someone picks up the check, and you lunge for it. Someone says your talk went well, and you list three things that went wrong. A neighbor brings soup when you're sick, and the first thing out of your mouth is, oh, you really shouldn't have, and the second is, I'll make it up to you. It sounds polite. It looks modest. Seneca, still in On Benefits, thinks it can be a quiet way of refusing the gift. Yesterday was the giver's half. Today is the harder half.
screen: `LUNGING FOR THE CHECK.` → `OH, YOU SHOULDN'T HAVE.` → `RECEIVING WELL.`

segments.voice: First, choose whom to owe. Be careful about whose favors you accept, Seneca says, even more careful than a giver is about whom to give to, because a benefit ties you to the giver. Take help from someone you don't respect, and you carry that tie around. Second, let the giver see it. When we accept, we should accept cheerfully and let our gladness show, so the giver gets an immediate return. Not a muttered thanks at the floor. A face that's actually glad. Third, the first installment. Whoever receives a benefit gratefully, Seneca says, has already paid the first installment on it. You can't always repay a favor in kind; some you never can. But receiving it gladly is a real part of the repayment, open to everyone, right away. Fourth, don't rush to pay it back. Someone too eager to repay, he warns, acts like an unwilling debtor, as if the favor were a weight to throw off fast. Racing to even the score can be a way of saying, I didn't want to owe you. So the person who lunges for the check isn't always being kind. Sometimes they're refusing to let someone else be kind. Seneca borrows a picture from the older Stoic Chrysippus: two people playing catch. The giver throws well, the receiver catches well, and the ball has to be caught before it can be thrown back.
screen: `CHOOSE WHOM TO OWE.` · `LET THE GIVER SEE IT.` · `GLAD RECEIVING PAYS THE FIRST PART.` · `DON'T RACE TO EVEN THE SCORE.` · then, large: `RECEIVE GLADLY.`

segments.voice: Bring back a gift you received recently and deflected: a compliment you argued with, help you waved away, a kindness you rushed to repay. Replay it, and this time just receive it, let your face show you're glad, say thank you, and stop there. Notice whether that feels exposed, and what it might give back to the other person.
Receiving well. Seneca says a gift received gladly, with the gladness showing, is already the first installment of the repayment. Today's word.
Your line: receive gladly. Letting someone be kind to you is a kindness too. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of On Benefits practice accepting help and compliments openly, thanking the giver with visible gladness instead of deflecting or rushing to repay.

original.note: Latin: pleasing, and also grateful. Seneca's line uses its adverb: whoever receives grate, gratefully, has paid the first installment.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the game-of-catch picture is credited to Chrysippus, as Seneca himself does (2.17); cut 'his most generous idea'; replaced the gratus/gratis etymology (gratis comes from gratia) with the word as Seneca uses it; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel; varied the stock 'Settle, and breathe' opener; softened 'often'.
2.18: be even more careful choosing whom to owe than whom to give to. Paraphrased; confirm section.
2.22: receive cheerfully and let joy be seen; whoever receives a benefit gratefully has paid its first installment (qui grate beneficium accipit, primam eius pensionem solvit). Confirm.
4.40: one who is too eager to repay is an unwilling debtor, and an unwilling debtor is ungrateful. Confirm section and wording of the paraphrase.
The ball-game image (Chrysippus' simile, retold by Seneca) is at On Benefits 2.17; confirm.
